1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to a square that adds control of d5 and b5 and commits White to nothing yet: a fianchetto, a quick central break or a solid pawn centre all stay possible. White keeps the first-move initiative in a symmetrical position and plays for a small, lasting edge.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Chooses the fianchetto: the king's bishop will watch the centre from g2 and White can castle early, with the d-pawn break held in reserve. It is slower than developing the knight first, and Black can mirror the set-up for a quiet manoeuvring game.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once and heads for an open game: after the trade of pawns White's knight recaptures on d4 with the extra move and a strong central post. White gives up the quiet manoeuvring of the other set-ups and has to show the open position pays.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White: the fianchetto prepares a bishop on the long diagonal, where it presses on the centre and the queenside, and gives the king a sound shelter. Black keeps the symmetry and invites a manoeuvring game in which White's extra move still counts.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on e4 and d5 and does not yet fix the pawn structure. Black can still fianchetto or strike in the centre, and avoids simply mirroring White, where White's extra move would tell.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 e5.strategy: Grabs space in the centre and takes d4 and f4 away from White's pieces. The price is a weak d5 square, which White's c-pawn already watches: Black signs up for a game in which White's pieces aim at that hole.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto. For now the knight on f3 blocks the bishop's long diagonal, but it points at the centre and starts to count as soon as the knight steps aside, and White is ready to castle.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the knight out first, adding control of d5 and e4 and leaving the bishop's move for later. The usual set-up still arises, with White flexible about how to handle the centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once, trading White's d-pawn for Black's c-pawn. White gets an open game with the extra move, but the bishop is not yet on g2 to support it, and Black's own fianchetto bishop will bear down the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Matches White's development. The bishop looks down the long diagonal towards the centre and the b2 pawn, backing the knight on c6 in the fight for d4. Nothing is committed in the centre, so the game stays level and strategic.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and presses on e4 and d5 while the bishop's route to g7 stays open. Black develops without hurry and contests the centre, but still needs the bishop move to complete the fianchetto.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 e5.strategy: Takes space in the centre and keeps White's knight out of d4. The cost is a weak d5 square, watched by the c4 pawn, and a king's bishop that will look at its own pawn on e5 once it reaches g7.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.strategy: Castles behind the fianchettoed bishop and brings the rook towards the centre. White has finished the kingside set-up and is free to choose where the knight and the d-pawn go; the game is symmetrical and decided by manoeuvring.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the second knight before castling, adding control of d5 and e4 and keeping the d-pawn flexible. The set-up is the same as with the castling move first; White only chooses the order.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: A quiet, flexible move: the pawn supports a later advance in the centre and gives the bishop on c1 its diagonal. White builds slowly and keeps the position closed, which concedes time to Black's mirrored set-up.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn, so White's pieces cannot settle there, and keeps a compact structure with the bishop's diagonal still open. Black leaves the later choice between a central break and queenside play open and meets White's set-up with a sturdy, flexible one.

Takes control of d5 and frees the e7 square for a knight, which keeps the bishop's long diagonal clear. A respected, flexible set-up that is a little slower and more passive in the centre than the pawn move to d6.

Brings out the last kingside piece and watches e4 and d5, so White cannot expand in the centre for free. Black prepares to castle and keeps the choice of pawn set-up for later; the knight blocks the bishop's diagonal for the time being.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Three Knights, Fianchetto Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.strategy: Brings the second knight into play and adds to the control of d5 and e4. White has castled and Black has not yet, in a mirror set-up; the c4 pawn gives White a little more space, and the game is balanced until one side finds a plan in the centre.

Supports a later advance in the centre and frees the bishop on c1, so White builds slowly behind the fianchetto. The cost is that White relies on manoeuvring, and Black's mirrored structure is just as solid.

Prepares to expand on the queenside with a rook on b1 and a pawn advance. White commits to play on the wing before the queen's knight is out, and Black gets time to develop the pieces and decide the centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Three Knights, Fianchetto Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.O-.strategy: Brings the knight out and puts pressure on d5, which Black's e-pawn already guards. White's c4 pawn restricts Black's d-pawn, so Black has to find the right moment to open the centre; the game is balanced.

Keeps the centre closed and frees the bishop on c1, and White builds without hurry. Against Black's pawn on e6, which guards d5 but shuts in the bishop on c8, the quiet set-up leaves White time to prepare a central break.
Prepares Bb2, but first it opens the long diagonal to the rook on a1, which nothing guards: Black's g7-bishop simply takes it with ...Bxa1.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Four Knights Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the centre: the knight watches e4 and d5, so White cannot advance in the centre for free. Black copies White's development and keeps the pawn structure flexible, accepting that White's extra move gives a slight, lasting edge.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and takes d4 away from White's pieces. Black accepts a weak d5 square, which White's pieces can aim at, in return for space and a firm grip on the centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Starts the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will press on d4 and the knight on c3 once the centre is clear. Black keeps the structure symmetrical and invites a manoeuvring game in which White's extra move still counts.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: The fianchetto set-up: the king's bishop will press on the centre from g2 and the king gets a shelter. It invites Black to challenge the centre at once, so it tests whether Black's pieces are placed well to strike at c4.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: Prepares a d-pawn advance with a solid pawn on e3 and opens the king's bishop. White heads for a classical pawn centre rather than a fianchetto, at the price of shutting in the queen's bishop for the time being.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre now that both sides have a knight out. After the pawn trade White's knight lands on d4 with the extra move, and the game opens into piece play where White's lead in space and time counts; Black can challenge the knight at once.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6.strategy: Mirrors White's solid set-up and opens the king's bishop. Black prepares to answer a central advance with a strike of its own in the centre; the price is a passive bishop on c8 for the time being.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 d5.strategy: Meets the quiet set-up with an immediate strike in the centre: the pawn attacks c4 and claims space before White's d-pawn can move. It trades the symmetry for activity, and the pawn on d5 must be kept defended if White builds up against it.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, but against a set-up aiming at the centre it is slow. White can build a broad pawn centre while the bishop waits behind its pawns; sound, but less purposeful than the central moves.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.strategy: Opens the centre now that both sides are developed: the pawn challenges c5, and White's extra move counts for more in an open position. Black has to decide how the centre is settled, and the symmetry of the pawns will not survive for long.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.a3.strategy: A waiting move with a purpose: it keeps Black's knight off b4 and prepares queenside space. White keeps every central plan open and loses little if Black commits first.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Be.strategy: A modest development that prepares quick castling. The bishop is solid on e2 but less active than elsewhere, and with the d-pawn still at home Black may claim the centre first.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.name: Tarrasch Defence: Symmetrical Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.background: Ding Liren played it against Hikaru Nakamura in their last game of the 2022 Candidates Tournament; the win helped him qualify for the 2023 World Chess Championship.
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.strategy: Meets the strike with one of its own: the pawn attacks c4 and claims the centre, so the c- and d-pawns now face each other. Black reaches a classical structure in which the result depends on how the tension is resolved.
Resolves the central tension at once, trading the c-pawn for White's d-pawn. White keeps a pawn on d4 if it recaptures with the e-pawn, while Black gets a half-open c-file to press on the c4 pawn.
Develops the bishop and prepares castling, but the knight on c6 is left to the thrust 6.d5. The pawn attacks the knight, and Black loses material whichever way it answers.
A quiet move with a plan: it prepares to take on c5 and then expand on the queenside, with the bishop landing on b2. If Black keeps the symmetry, White's extra move tells.

Resolves the tension on White's terms: if Black recaptures with the e-pawn, taking on c5 can leave Black with an isolated pawn on d5. A direct, principled exchange, though it also lets Black's pieces develop freely.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Semi-Tarrasch Defence, with e3
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.strategy: Develops the bishop to a natural square where it eyes h7, keeps the tension in the centre and prepares castling. It is less direct than resolving the centre at once and leaves Black to choose how to release the tension.

Trades off the pawn that White wants to take on c5, so the plan of capturing it and expanding on the queenside gains nothing. Black gives up the tension in the centre and White recaptures with a free hand.

Takes b5 away from White's pieces and prepares queenside expansion, but it is a waiting move in a symmetrical centre. White can take on c5 and gain space with a pawn on b4, where the extra tempo tells.
Takes the c-pawn so that White's bishop must recapture on c4, which uses up the time White spent on a3. White's bishop gets an active post in return, and Black can then challenge the pawn on d4.
Mirrors White's bishop and aims at h2, keeping the symmetry and getting ready to castle. Tension remains in the centre on both wings, so neither side has committed to a structure yet.

Wins a tempo against the bishop: it is attacked and must go to c4 to recover the pawn, after which Black challenges the pawn on d4 and finishes development. White is left with a central pawn that may become isolated; Black gets an easy, equal game.
Trades Black's c-pawn for White's d-pawn at once. White can recapture with the e-pawn, leaving a pawn on d4 that may become isolated, while Black keeps the option of taking on c4 whenever it suits.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.name: Tarrasch Defence: Symmetrical Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.d4.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn and keeps a pawn in the centre, accepting that White can take on c5 and leave Black with an isolated pawn on d5. In return Black's pieces are active and the d5 pawn controls the e4 and c4 squares.
Recaptures with the knight, so no isolated pawn arises for Black. The knight is centralised but can be challenged, and White can pin the knight on c6 against the king; Black has to develop with care.
Hangs the queen: the knight on c3 takes it, and Black recaptures only a knight and a pawn for it.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once: the pawn attacks c4, which nothing protects yet, so White must react. Black takes the initiative and tests whether White's fianchetto leaves the centre without a fight.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors the fianchetto and leaves the centre alone for now. A flexible set-up that is safe on the kingside but gives White the choice of how to fight for the centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 e6.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Four Knights Variation, Keres-Parma System
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 e6.strategy: A modest set-up: the pawn covers d5, opens the king's bishop and prepares to castle without committing the d-pawn. Black postpones the fight for the centre and accepts a slightly cramped position for solidity.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d4.strategy: Answers the strike in the centre rather than defending c4: the pawn attacks c5 and opens lines for White's pieces, accepting that the c-pawn may be given up for activity. White wants open play against Black's centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.strategy: Takes the central pawn at once instead of letting the d-pawn cramp White. The c-pawn is traded for Black's d-pawn, so the c4 pawn is no longer a target, and Black's knight must recapture into the centre, where White can challenge it.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.Bg.strategy: Finishes the fianchetto but lets Black gain space: the d-pawn can advance and drive the knight from c3. White gets a solid set-up in return, but the central pawn grip passes to Black.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d4.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d4.strategy: Settles the tension in the centre and leaves the pawn on d4 guarded by the knight on c6, so White has to recapture with a piece. The c4 pawn is still attacked by the d-pawn, so White cannot take time over the recapture.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d4.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Semi-Tarrasch Defence
1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d4.strategy: A solid reply: the e-pawn guards d5 and Black keeps the tension on c4 and d4. Black accepts a slightly passive bishop on c8 in return for a firm centre and a safe position.
Takes the c4 pawn, but White strikes with d5 against the knight on c6 and regains it with a lead in development and more space. Black ends up with a worse game and nothing to show for it.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 g6 5.Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto, with the bishop looking at the centre from g2 and the king ready to castle. Both sides have chosen the same set-up, so the game turns on subtle differences in piece placement.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 g6 5.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once instead of finishing the fianchetto first. Trading White's d-pawn for Black's c-pawn opens the game and gives White's knight a central post, at the cost of letting Black develop easily.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 g6 5.d3.strategy: Keeps the centre closed and prepares to bring the pieces out behind the fianchetto. It is slow and flexible, but lets Black take the initiative in the centre.

1.Nf3 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 g6 5.Bg.strategy: Completes Black's mirror fianchetto: the bishop covers the long diagonal and d4, and the king will be safe after castling. Full symmetry holds the balance, and the game becomes a long strategic fight with equal chances.

Builds the compact pawn chain first: the d6 pawn takes e5 away from White's knight and frees the bishop on c8. Black accepts a little less central space in return for a position without weaknesses, and waits for White to show a plan.

Challenges the centre at once instead of copying White. If White takes, Black recaptures with the knight, which the knight on c3 attacks immediately; Black gets an active game, but the king and the king's bishop are still at home and the centre knight needs care.
